title: ref, in, and out
hook: After ordinary parameters, C# lets a parameter alias a caller’s variable. ref is read-write aliasing. in is a readonly alias. out is a definite-assignment obligation. These are language features, not C++ references with destructor rules.

sections.heading: Why they exist
sections.prose: Ordinary by-value passing is the default and the right default. ref exists so Try-style APIs and interop can write back to a local without wrapping a class. out is the definite-assignment variant: the caller may pass an unassigned local; the callee must assign before return. in (and ref readonly) exist so a large struct can be passed without copying, provided nobody mutates it through that alias.

sections.heading: Defensive copies and readonly struct
sections.prose: If you pass a mutable struct as in, the compiler may copy it anyway so a method cannot mutate the caller’s value through a sneaky instance method. Mark the struct readonly (next struct topic) so in is a true zero-copy readonly view. That matters on a high-concurrency attempt-submit path where cache-key structs are compared in a loop. Do not sprinkle ref on class parameters to “go faster” — classes are already a reference.

snippets.label: out for parse, in for a readonly key
snippets.explanation: TryParse uses out so the local can start unassigned. in CacheKey avoids copying a readonly struct into Exists. ContainsKey still uses equality — module 05.

sections.heading: Interview traps
sections.prose: ref requires the caller to pass a definitely assigned variable and to write ref at the call site. You cannot pass a property as ref or out because a property is not a storage location. C# 14 lets lambda parameters take ref/in/out modifiers without repeating types. Extension members that wrap these tricks wait for module 10.

interviewTakeaways: ref aliases storage; in is readonly alias; out must be assigned by the callee.
in plus a mutable struct can still copy; readonly struct is the matching design.
commonPitfalls: Using ref on reference types as a cargo-cult performance habit.
Forgetting that TryParse-style out parameters leave the value undefined on failure unless the callee assigned it — good APIs assign default on failure.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS always passes object references and copies primitives. There is no out or in. Multiple outputs use objects or arrays.
TS/JS prefer returning a tuple or Result object. C# still uses out in the BCL (TryParse) and tuples when you want two values without aliasing.
